title: Galileo and His Daughter Maria Celeste
text:
Galileo Galilei never married, but he had three children with Marina Gamba. His two daughters, being illegitimate, had little chance of a good marriage, and when they were young girls he placed them in the convent of San Matteo at Arcetri, near Florence. The elder, Virginia, took the name Suor Maria Celeste.

She was intelligent, devoted and practical. From 1623 she wrote to her father regularly, and 124 of her letters survive, though his replies are lost. She made him candied fruit and medicines, mended and washed his collars, and worried about his health. He sent the poor convent food and wine and helped it with money and favors. In 1631 he rented a villa near the convent to be close to her.

In 1633 Galileo was tried in Rome by the Inquisition for his support of the idea that the earth moves around the sun. He was forced to recant and was sentenced to house arrest, with the penance of reciting the seven penitential psalms every week for three years. Maria Celeste wrote to him with comfort and news, and obtained permission to say the psalms for him herself.

In December 1633 he was allowed to return to his villa at Arcetri. They had only a few months together. In April 1634 she fell ill and died, at thirty-three. Galileo wrote to a friend of his immense sadness and that he felt her continually calling him.
lesson: A child's love can sustain a parent through disgrace when the world turns away. The small, practical care we give each other often matters most.
source: Letters of Suor Maria Celeste to Galileo; Dava Sobel, Galileo's Daughter (1999)
